content.title: About
content.content: Baby Toddler Pears, Stage 1 are soft, ripe pears that have been peeled and cut into small pieces suitable for infants aged 6 to 12 months. They are gently heat‑treated to ensure safety for first foods.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Pears are rich in dietary fiber, which supports a healthy digestive system in babies.
They contain vitamin C that helps strengthen the immune system.
Pears have a low allergenic potential and are often recommended as a first fruit.
Heat treatment retains most of the natural flavor and aroma.
Pears are easily digested and rarely cause constipation in infants.

items.title: High in vitamin C
items.content: Vitamin C supports immune function and aids iron absorption.

items.title: Contains dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber promotes healthy digestion and helps prevent constipation.

items.title: Low sugar content
items.content: Pears are naturally sweet but contain less sugar than many other fruits, making them gentle on a baby’s stomach.

items.title: Source of potassium
items.content: Potassium helps regulate fluid balance and supports heart function.

items.title: Supports flavor development
items.content: The mild sweet taste helps infants become accustomed to new foods.

items.title: Allergic reaction
items.content: Although rare, monitor the baby for any signs of allergy when introducing pears for the first time.

items.title: Choking hazard
items.content: Pieces must be fully softened and free of large chunks to avoid choking.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Excessive consumption may contribute to tooth decay, so offer in moderation.

items.title: Storage concerns
items.content: Improper storage can lead to bacterial growth; always check the expiration date.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the pears as a smooth puree or finely mashed pieces. You may thin the puree with breast milk or formula for a smoother texture if needed.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep refrigerated at 0‑4 °C in an airtight container for up to 3 days. Frozen portions can be stored for up to 2 months.

content.title: About
content.content: Soy bread is a whole‑grain loaf that incorporates soy flour or soy protein. It has a soft crumb, a mild nutty flavor, and a high amount of plant‑based protein. The bread is popular in dietetic and vegetarian diets.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Soy bread contains more protein than traditional wheat bread.
Soy protein improves dough elasticity, giving a chewier texture.
In several countries soy bread is a traditional staple during fasting periods.
Soybeans are rich in isoflavones, which may support hormonal balance.
Soy bread often has a longer shelf life due to its lower moisture content.

items.title: Rich in plant protein
items.content: Soy bread provides about 12–15 g of protein per 100 g, helping maintain muscle mass.

items.title: Contains isoflavones
items.content: Isoflavones act as antioxidants and may benefit cardiovascular health.

items.title: Low glycemic index
items.content: Compared with white bread, soy bread raises blood sugar more slowly.

items.title: Source of dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber supports digestion and promotes satiety.

items.title: High in B‑vitamins
items.content: Vitamins B1, B2 and B6 are involved in energy metabolism.

items.title: Soy allergy
items.content: People allergic to soy may experience reactions ranging from skin rash to anaphylaxis when consuming soy bread.

items.title: Phytic acid content
items.content: Phytic acid can reduce the absorption of certain minerals, so a varied diet is recommended.

items.title: Potential high sodium in some recipes
items.content: Certain soy breads contain added salt; individuals with hypertension should check the label.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Soy bread can be enjoyed like any other loaf – in sandwiches, toasted, with soups or salads. It also works well for making breadcrumbs or as a high‑protein base for open‑face sandwiches.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store soy bread in an airtight container at room temperature for up to 3 days. For longer storage keep it refrigerated (up to 7 days) or freeze sliced pieces.

double-cheeseburger-on-wheat-bun-2-mediu.title: Double Cheeseburger on Wheat Bun, 2 Medium Patties

content.title: About
content.content: The double cheeseburger consists of a wheat bun, two medium beef patties, cheddar cheese, lettuce, tomato, onion, pickles and sauce. Each burger weighs about 250 g and provides roughly 680 kcal.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The wheat bun gives a soft texture and a subtle grain aroma.
Combining two patties with cheddar makes the burger more filling and boosts protein content.
The classic American cheeseburger appeared in the 1920s; the double version became popular in the 1970s.
Cheddar melts at around 30 °C, creating a stretchy layer.
The burger is often served with french fries and a soft drink.

items.title: High protein content
items.content: Two beef patties provide about 30 g of protein, essential for muscle repair.

items.title: Source of iron
items.content: Beef is rich in heme iron, which is readily absorbed by the body.

items.title: Calcium from cheese
items.content: Cheddar cheese adds calcium that supports bone and tooth health.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Beef and cheese supply vitamin B12 and other B‑vitamins important for the nervous system.

items.title: Energy boost
items.content: The burger quickly replenishes energy thanks to its mix of protein, fat and carbohydrates.

items.title: High calorie and fat content
items.content: A double cheeseburger can contain over 600 kcal and a notable amount of saturated fat, which may be undesirable in excess.

items.title: Sodium level
items.content: Sauce and cheese add a lot of salt, which can be an issue for people with hypertension.

items.title: Dairy allergy
items.content: Cheddar may trigger allergic reactions in individuals with lactose intolerance or milk protein allergy.

items.title: Food safety
items.content: Undercooked patties may harbor pathogenic bacteria; they should be cooked to an internal temperature of 71 °C.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the burger hot, split the bun, add sauce to taste. It is convenient to eat with hands, but a fork and knife can be used if the bun is very soft.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Prepared burgers are best eaten immediately. If needed, store in the refrigerator for no more than 24 hours in an airtight container. Reheat in an oven or microwave to an internal temperature of 71 °C.

content.title: About
content.content: An egg omelet with fresh vegetables (excluding dark‑green leafy veg and tomatoes) is a nutritious dish that provides protein, vitamins, and minerals. When cooked with a small amount of oil, it fits well into a balanced diet.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Eggs are one of the most affordable sources of complete protein.
The omelet can be quickly customized with different vegetables to suit personal taste.
Compared with fried eggs, an omelet is usually fluffier due to whisking.
Vegetables such as bell pepper, onion, and carrot add color and aroma.
Omelet‑making traditions exist worldwide: French, Spanish, Japanese, and more.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: Eggs contain all essential amino acids, supporting tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: Eggs provide B12, riboflavin, and folate, which are important for energy metabolism.

items.title: Contains vitamin D
items.content: The yolk is one of the few natural food sources of vitamin D, beneficial for bone health and immunity.

items.title: Vegetables add fiber and antioxidants
items.content: Bell pepper, carrot, and onion are rich in vitamin C, beta‑carotene, and phytochemicals.

items.title: Low in saturated fat
items.content: When cooked with a modest amount of plant oil, the omelet remains moderate in fat content.

items.title: Egg allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to egg proteins.

items.title: Cholesterol content
items.content: The yolk contains cholesterol; people with high cholesterol should limit yolk intake.

items.title: Foodborne infection
items.content: Undercooked eggs can harbor Salmonella; ensure eggs are fully cooked.

items.title: Excess sodium
items.content: If salt is added, monitor the amount to stay within recommended daily limits.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Beat eggs with a splash of milk, stir in diced vegetables (bell pepper, onion, carrot). Heat 1‑2 tsp of vegetable oil in a non‑stick pan, pour the mixture, and cook over medium heat, gently lifting the edges until set but still tender inside.

content.title: Storage
content.content: The omelet is best enjoyed fresh. If needed, store in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 24 hours; reheat before serving.
